chapters.title: Wait and Hope
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, waiting is not sitting idle: it is being stretched toward God like a cord pulled tight
chapters.trueMeaning: Stretched toward God, holding on, enduring
chapters.nutshell: In English, “wait” sounds passive and “hope” sounds like a wish. The Hebrew *qavah* is linked with *tiqvah*, a word that means both “hope” and “cord”, and pictures someone stretched toward God with eager expectation. The Greek words add endurance (*hypomonē*, “remaining under” a load), welcome and eager longing.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical waiting is active, confident hope that holds on to God and keeps faithful under pressure until he acts.
skeleton: We picture waiting as idle and hope as a wish
Qavah: stretched toward God; tiqvah is both hope and cord
Yachal, chakah and dumiyyah: hoping, longing and silent trust
God himself waits to be gracious (Isaiah 30:18)
Greek hypomonē is endurance under a load; other words add welcome and eager expectation
Translations each catch part of the picture: wait, hope, patience
Farmers, watchmen, soldiers and sailors show what waiting looks like
Jesus' followers wait actively, with endurance, for the hope of Israel

sections.h: The English words and what we assume
p: For most of us, **waiting** is something we put up with. We wait at a bus stop, in a queue or in a doctor's waiting room, doing nothing until something happens. And **hope** is often a soft wish: “I hope it doesn't rain tomorrow.” It may happen, it may not.

So when we read “they that wait upon the LORD” (Isaiah 40:31, KJV), we can easily picture someone sitting still and passive. When we read about hope, we may hear uncertainty. The Hebrew and Greek words are much stronger. They describe **tension, expectation, endurance and confidence**: a person leaning forward toward God, sure that he will keep his word.

sections.h: Qavah: stretched toward God
p: The main Hebrew verb is *qavah* (קָוָה), “to wait for, to look eagerly for, to hope”. Standard lexicons connect it with the noun *tiqvah* (תִּקְוָה), “hope”, and many scholars connect it with *qav* (קַו), a builder's **measuring line** (Jeremiah 31:39; Isaiah 28:17). The idea often suggested is of something **stretched or twisted tight**, like a cord pulled toward its goal.

One story makes the link vivid. The spies tell Rahab to tie “this **line** (*tiqvat*) of scarlet thread in the window” (Joshua 2:18, 21). The same word that usually means “hope” here means a **cord**. For Rahab, that red cord *was* her hope: the sign that she and her family would be saved when Jericho fell.

Isaiah says, “they who **wait for** the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31). The psalmist urges, “**Wait for** the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!” (Psalm 27:14). Notice how waiting goes with strength and courage. It is not weakness but leaning your whole weight on God's promise.
> To *qavah* is to be like a rope pulled tight between you and God's promise: the tension is part of the hope.

sections.h: Yachal, chakah and dumiyyah: hope, longing and silence
p: *Yachal* (יָחַל) means “to wait with hope”, often through a long, painful time. “I **wait** for the LORD, my soul **waits**, and in his word I **hope**” (Psalm 130:5). Here *qavah* comes twice and *yachal* once. The next verse adds a picture: “my soul waits for the Lord more than **watchmen for the morning**” (Psalm 130:6). Then the whole people is invited: “O Israel, **hope** in the LORD” (Psalm 130:7).

*Chakah* (חָכָה) means “to wait for, to long for”. Its most surprising use is about God: “Therefore the LORD **waits** to be gracious to you… blessed are all those who **wait** for him” (Isaiah 30:18). God waits for his people as they wait for him. Habakkuk hears about God's vision: “If it seems slow, **wait** for it; it will surely come” (Habakkuk 2:3).

*Dumiyyah* (דּוּמִיָּה) means **silence** or stillness, from a root meaning “to be still, quiet”. Psalm 62:1 says literally, “Only toward God is my soul **silence**.” This is the waiting of someone who has stopped arguing and struggling. Lamentations joins two of these words: “It is good that one should **hope** (*yachil*) and wait **quietly** (*dumam*) for the salvation of the LORD” (Lamentations 3:26).

sections.h: The Greek words: endurance, welcome and eager expectation
p: When Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), they often rendered *qavah* with *hypomenō* (ὑπομένω), as in Isaiah 40:31. The word means literally “to **remain under**”: to stay in place under a heavy load instead of running away. Its noun *hypomonē* (ὑπομονή) is **endurance, steadfastness**. Paul says that “suffering produces **endurance**, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope” (Romans 5:3–4), and James says “the testing of your faith produces **steadfastness**” (James 1:3).

*Prosdechomai* (προσδέχομαι) means both “to **wait for**” and “to **welcome, receive**”. Simeon was “**waiting for** the consolation of Israel” and Anna spoke to all who were “**waiting for** the redemption of Jerusalem” (Luke 2:25, 38). The same verb is used when critics say of Jesus, “This man **receives** sinners” (Luke 15:2). Waiting for God is like preparing to welcome an honoured guest.

*Apekdechomai* (ἀπεκδέχομαι) is **eager, intense** waiting. “The creation **waits with eager longing** for the revealing of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19), and “we wait eagerly for adoption as sons” (Romans 8:23). The noun in Romans 8:19, *apokaradokia* (ἀποκαραδοκία), is often explained as watching with the **head stretched forward**. *Anamenō* (ἀναμένω) is to wait for someone expected: believers “**wait for** his Son from heaven” (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

The everyday Greek word for hope is *elpis* (ἐλπίς). In ordinary Greek it could mean any **expectation**, even the expectation of something bad. In the Bible it becomes a **confident expectation of God's good**, resting on his promises: “we have this as a sure and steadfast **anchor** of the soul” (Hebrews 6:19).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: English has no single word that carries both “wait” and “hope” the way *qavah* does. So translators must choose. The **KJV** and **ESV** say “they that **wait upon/for** the LORD” in Isaiah 40:31, keeping the idea of time and patience. The **NIV** says “those who **hope** in the LORD”, which catches the eager expectation. Both are honest choices, and each hides half of the picture. Reading two versions side by side helps.

In Psalm 62:1 the **KJV** says “Truly my soul **waiteth** upon God”, the **NIV** “Truly my soul **finds rest** in God”, and the **ESV** “For God alone my soul **waits in silence**”. The Hebrew noun is “silence”, which is hard to put into a natural English sentence, so translators use “wait” or “rest”. The ESV keeps the silence most clearly.

In Romans 5:3 the **KJV** says “tribulation worketh **patience**”. This follows a long chain: the Latin Vulgate rendered *hypomonē* with *patientia* (from *patior*, “to suffer, endure”), and in older English “patience” meant **bearing suffering**. Today “patience” sounds like calmly waiting in a queue, so the **NIV** says “perseverance” and the **ESV** “endurance”. The Greek word is closer to a soldier holding his ground than to someone politely waiting.

The word **hope** itself has weakened in modern English. Translators keep it because it is the natural word, but readers need to remember that biblical hope is **confident**: it is as sure as the God who promised.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In the land of Israel, life depended on rain. Farmers sowed and then waited for “the early rain and the later rain” (Deuteronomy 11:14). James uses this picture: “See how the farmer **waits** for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains” (James 5:7). This kind of waiting is full of work and trust: you plough and sow, and then you trust God for what only he can give.

Cities had **watchmen** on the walls through the night. They could not make the sun rise, but they stayed awake and alert until it did (Psalm 130:6; Isaiah 21:11–12, “Watchman, what of the night?”). Israel also knew long waiting as a people: in slavery in Egypt, and in exile in Babylon, waiting for God to bring them home.

In the Greco-Roman world, *hypomonē* was praised as a manly virtue, like a soldier who **stands his post** and does not run. In Jewish writings such as 4 Maccabees it describes the endurance of the martyrs under torture. The **anchor** of Hebrews 6:19 comes from the world of sea travel, where an anchor holds a ship steady in a storm. And an old Greek story told of Pandora's jar, in which only *elpis* was left inside; Greeks argued whether hope was a blessing or a cruel trick. The Bible gives hope a firm ground: God's faithfulness.

sections.h: Waiting in Jewish prayer: the hope of Israel
p: Waiting for God's saving action runs through Jewish prayer. The dying Jacob cries out, “I **wait** for your salvation, O LORD” (Genesis 49:18). In the daily Amidah prayer, Jews ask God to make the branch of David flourish, “for we **hope** for your salvation all the day” (*ki lishuatkha qivvinu kol hayom*, using *qavah*). The well-known creed *Ani Ma'amin* says of the Messiah, “though he tarry, nevertheless I **wait** for him (*achakeh lo*) every day he may come.”

The national anthem of modern Israel is called *Hatikvah*, “**The Hope**”. It began as a nineteenth-century poem saying “our hope is not yet lost”, the hope of returning to the land after centuries of exile. The word chosen for that song is the same *tiqvah* that once hung as a cord in Rahab's window.

The apostle Paul speaks in this same Jewish voice. On trial he says he is judged “because of my **hope in the promise** made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day” (Acts 26:6–7). In Rome he says, “It is because of the **hope of Israel** that I am wearing this chain” (Acts 28:20). Christian hope is not a new, private idea; it is Israel's hope fulfilled in the Messiah.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: waiting with endurance
p: Before Pentecost, the risen Jesus told his disciples “to **wait for** the promise of the Father” (Acts 1:4). They did not wait idly: they gathered and “devoted themselves to prayer” (Acts 1:14). Waiting and praying belong together. Ten days later the Spirit came, and the waiting church became a witnessing church.

Jesus himself is the great example of *hypomonē*: “for the joy that was set before him he **endured** the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). So believers are told to “run with **endurance** the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1). James points to the prophets and to Job: “You have heard of the **steadfastness** of Job” (James 5:11). Job did not wait quietly; he argued and cried out, but he did not let go of God.

Paul ties the whole creation into this waiting. Creation groans like a woman in labour, and “we ourselves… groan inwardly as we **wait eagerly**” (Romans 8:22–23). “If we hope for what we do not see, we **wait for it with patience**” (Romans 8:25). The early church lived “**waiting for** our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13).

sections.h: Living it out
p: Biblical waiting is not giving up or doing nothing. Like the farmer, you keep doing your part faithfully while trusting God for what only he can do. Like the watchman, you stay awake and alert. Like Simeon and Anna, you keep worshipping and get ready to **welcome** what God will bring.

When waiting is hard, the Psalms give permission to be honest and also to be still. You can cry out like Job and still hold on to God like Rahab's cord. And remember Isaiah 30:18: while you wait for God, **God is waiting to be gracious to you**. Hope is not a wish in the dark; it is a rope tied to the faithful God.

chapters.title: Prophets and Prophecy
chapters.subtitle: A biblical prophet is first God's spokesperson calling people back to the covenant, not mainly a fortune-teller
chapters.trueMeaning: God's spokesperson speaking forth his word
chapters.nutshell: Today “prophecy” usually means predicting the future. In the Bible a prophet (*navi*) is above all God's **spokesperson**: Aaron was Moses' *navi* because he spoke for him. Prophets did foretell events, but their main work was to forth-tell God's word, calling Israel back to covenant faithfulness, and New Testament prophecy aims to build up, encourage and comfort.
chapters.bigIdea: A prophet speaks on God's behalf to call his people back to faithful covenant life, and prediction serves that purpose.
skeleton: We think of prophecy as predicting the future
Navi: a spokesperson, as Aaron was for Moses
Seers, oracles and “Thus says the LORD”: the prophet as God's messenger
Greek prophētēs: one who speaks forth on behalf of a god
Translators choose between burden, oracle and prophecy

Listening to and testing prophetic words today

sections.h: The English word and what we assume
p: In everyday English a **prophecy** is a prediction, and a prophet is someone who tells the future. Many Christians read the prophets mainly as a puzzle of predictions about the end times, and they imagine prophetic ministry today as revealing secrets about people's futures.

The Bible does contain real predictions, and the New Testament sees many of them fulfilled in Jesus. But the Hebrew and Greek words put the weight somewhere else. A prophet is first **someone who speaks for God**. Most of what the prophets said was about the present: justice, idolatry, care for the poor, faithfulness to the covenant. Prediction usually served that message: “If you turn back, this will happen; if not, that will happen.”

sections.h: Navi: God's spokesperson
p: The main Hebrew word is *navi* (נָבִיא). Scholars debate its root. Many connect it with an old Akkadian verb meaning “to call”, so a *navi* may be “**one who is called**” or “**one who calls out, announces**”. Both fit the Bible: the prophet is called by God and then speaks for him.

The clearest definition is in a story. Moses fears he cannot speak to Pharaoh, so God says, “See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be **your prophet**” (Exodus 7:1). Earlier God had said that Aaron “shall be your **mouth**” (Exodus 4:16). A *navi* is a **mouth**: someone who passes on another's words.

God promises Moses, “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will **put my words in his mouth**, and he shall speak to them all that I command him” (Deuteronomy 18:18). The activity is called *nevu'ah* (נְבוּאָה), “prophecy”, and the verb is *nibba* / *hitnabbe*, “to prophesy”.
> A prophet is not first a fortune-teller. He is a messenger with a mouth full of God's words.

sections.h: Seers, oracles and “Thus says the LORD”
p: Older titles stress **seeing**. “Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, ‘Come, let us go to the **seer**,’ for today's ‘prophet’ was formerly called a seer” (1 Samuel 9:9). The word there is *ro'eh* (רֹאֶה), “one who sees”. Another word, *chozeh* (חֹזֶה), “visionary”, is used of Gad, “David's seer” (2 Samuel 24:11), and Isaiah's book begins, “The **vision** (*chazon*) of Isaiah” (Isaiah 1:1). The prophet sees what God shows and then says it.

A prophet's message is often called a *massa* (מַשָּׂא), from *nasa*, “to lift, carry”. It may mean a message **lifted up** with the voice, or a **load** laid on the prophet. Jeremiah 23:33–38 plays on this double sense: when people mockingly ask, “What is the burden of the LORD?”, God answers that the people themselves have become the burden he will cast off.

Prophets often begin with *koh amar YHWH* (כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה), “**Thus says the LORD**”. This was the language of royal messengers: an envoy would stand before a city and say, “Thus says the great king” (2 Kings 18:19). Prophets were also called *ish ha'elohim* (אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים), “**man of God**”: Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6), Elijah (1 Kings 17:24) and Elisha (2 Kings 4:9).

sections.h: What the prophets actually did: covenant forth-telling
p: The prophets were **messengers of the covenant**. God says he warned Israel “by every prophet and every seer, saying, ‘**Turn** from your evil ways and keep my commandments’” (2 Kings 17:13). Their constant call was *shuv*, “return”. Micah sums it up: “do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). Amos cries, “let justice roll down like waters” (Amos 5:24).

Often they spoke like lawyers in a court case. “The LORD has a **controversy** with the inhabitants of the land” (Hosea 4:1); “Hear what the LORD says: Arise, plead your case before the mountains” (Micah 6:1). The Hebrew *riv* means a legal dispute: God brings a covenant lawsuit against his people.

Even predictions of judgment were usually **conditional**. God says through Jeremiah, “If at any time I declare concerning a nation… that I will pluck up and break down… and if that nation… turns from its evil, I will relent” (Jeremiah 18:7–8). Jonah announced, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!” Nineveh repented, and God spared it (Jonah 3:4–10). The prophecy succeeded because it brought repentance, not because it came true word for word.

Moses even wished that every Israelite could share this gift: “Would that all the LORD's people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29). Joel promised that one day God would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28).

sections.h: The Greek words: speaking forth
p: The Septuagint translated *navi* with *prophētēs* (προφήτης). It comes from *pro* and *phēmi*, “to speak”. In this word *pro* mainly means “**forth**” or “**on behalf of**”, not only “before in time”. So a *prophētēs* is **one who speaks out for someone else**, especially for a god.

The verb is *prophēteuō* (προφητεύω), “to prophesy”, and the noun *prophēteia* (προφητεία), “prophecy”. Paul defines the purpose of prophecy in the church: “the one who **prophesies** speaks to people for their **upbuilding** and **encouragement** and **consolation**” (1 Corinthians 14:3). The three Greek words are *oikodomē* (building up), *paraklēsis* (encouragement, exhortation) and *paramythia* (comfort). Prediction is not even mentioned.

Prophecy is also to be **tested**. “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said” (1 Corinthians 14:29). “Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). Jesus warns about false prophets and says, “You will recognize them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:15–16).

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: The biggest loss is not a single verse but the English word itself. **“Prophecy”** has drifted toward “prediction”, so readers hear *fore*-telling when the Bible usually means *forth*-telling. Translators keep “prophet” because it is the traditional word that runs from Greek through Latin (*propheta*) into English, and there is no better single word. “Spokesperson” would sound like a press officer.

For *massa*, the **KJV** says “The **burden** of Babylon” (Isaiah 13:1), the **ESV** “The **oracle** concerning Babylon”, and the **NIV** “A **prophecy** against Babylon”. “Burden” keeps the picture of a load; “oracle” and “prophecy” give the sense for modern readers. Scholars still debate which picture the word carries, so each version is making a reasonable choice.

The verb *hitnabbe* can describe wild, ecstatic behaviour. Of Saul, troubled by an evil spirit, the **KJV** says “he **prophesied** in the midst of the house” and the **NIV** “he was **prophesying** in his house”, while the **ESV** says “he **raved** within his house” (1 Samuel 18:10). The ESV chooses the meaning that fits the scene; the others keep the same word so you can see it is the prophetic verb.

In 1 Corinthians 14:3 the **KJV** says “**edification**, and exhortation, and comfort”. “Edification” comes from the Latin *aedificatio*, “building a house”. It is correct, but few readers now hear the building picture, so the **ESV** says “upbuilding” and the **NIV** “strengthening”.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In ancient Israel prophets stood close to power. Nathan rebuked King David to his face: “**You are the man!**” (2 Samuel 12:7). Elijah confronted Ahab, and Jeremiah told kings what they did not want to hear. In a culture of **honour and shame**, publicly calling a king to repent was dangerous. Jesus said, “it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem” (Luke 13:33).

There were groups called “**the sons of the prophets**” (2 Kings 2:3), probably disciples who lived and learned around a prophet like Elisha. So when Amos says, “I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but I was a herdsman” (Amos 7:14), he means he was not a professional; God simply took him from the flock. Prophets also acted out their messages: Jeremiah wore a yoke (Jeremiah 27:2), and Ezekiel lay beside a model of besieged Jerusalem (Ezekiel 4).

In the Hebrew Bible the second section is called *Nevi'im*, “**the Prophets**”. It includes the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings), because telling Israel's history in the light of the covenant is prophetic work, and the Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve). In the synagogue, the Torah reading is followed by a reading from the Prophets, the *Haftarah*. That is what Jesus did in Nazareth when he read from Isaiah (Luke 4:16–21; compare Acts 13:15, “after the reading from the Law and the Prophets”).

In the Greek world, a *prophētēs* was the official at an oracle, such as Delphi, who spoke out or interpreted the god's message to those who came to ask. Rabbinic tradition taught that after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi the holy spirit of prophecy departed from Israel (Talmud Yoma 9b), and 1 Maccabees speaks of waiting “until a prophet should come” (1 Maccabees 4:46). That is why John the Baptist and Jesus caused such excitement.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: the prophet like Moses
p: Crowds recognised Jesus as a prophet. “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee” (Matthew 21:11). The disciples on the road to Emmaus called him “a prophet mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19). After he fed the five thousand, people said, “This is indeed **the Prophet who is to come** into the world” (John 6:14), and Peter applied Deuteronomy 18 to him (Acts 3:22).

Jesus acted like the prophets. He called Israel to repent, he spoke for the poor, and he performed prophetic sign-actions, such as cleansing the Temple while quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer… but you make it a den of robbers” (Mark 11:17; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11). Like the prophets, he was rejected in his home town: “A prophet is not without honour, except in his hometown” (Mark 6:4).

At Pentecost Peter announced that Joel's promise had come true: God had poured out his Spirit, and now sons and daughters, young and old, would **prophesy** (Acts 2:16–18). Moses' wish was fulfilled. The church had prophets (Acts 13:1; 21:9), and Paul urged all believers to “earnestly desire to prophesy” (1 Corinthians 14:1), always for the building up of the community.

sections.h: Living it out
p: Reading the prophets as God's spokesmen changes how we read them. Instead of only asking “What does this predict?”, ask “What is God calling his people to turn from and turn to?” Their words about justice, idolatry, mercy and faithfulness speak directly to the church today.

Prophetic speech in the church should **build up, encourage and comfort**. It should be humble and tested, and it should point people back to God and his word. Every believer can share in this when we speak God's truth in love, sometimes comforting, sometimes challenging, always calling one another back to the covenant God who loves us.

chapters.title: Condemnation, Guilt and Chastisement
chapters.subtitle: Courtroom words in the Bible: who is in the right, who is in the wrong, and how God disciplines in order to heal
chapters.trueMeaning: A verdict of “in the wrong”; liability; corrective discipline
chapters.nutshell: We often hear “condemnation” as God's final rejection and “guilt” as a bad feeling. In Hebrew, to condemn (*hirshia*) is a judge's verdict that someone is **in the wrong**, and *asham* is guilt that must be **repaired**. The Greek separates “judging” (*krinō*) from “condemning” (*katakrinō*), and its word for chastening (*paideuō*) means **training a child**.
chapters.bigIdea: In Christ there is no condemning verdict, and God's judging and chastening aim to set things right and heal, not to destroy.

sections.h: The English words and what we assume
p: For many Christians, **condemnation** means God's final rejection, being sent to hell. **Guilt** is a heavy feeling of being bad. **Chastisement** sounds like a beating. Put together, these words can make God sound like an angry judge waiting to punish.

The Bible's words come mostly from the **law court** and the **family**. In court, the question is: who is in the right and who is in the wrong, and what must be done to put things right? In the family, the question is: how does a loving father train his child? When we hear these words in their own setting, they become less frightening and more hopeful, without losing their seriousness.

sections.h: Hirshia: the verdict “in the wrong”
p: The adjective *rasha* (רָשָׁע) usually means “wicked”, but in a legal case it means simply “**in the wrong**, guilty”. Its opposite is *tsaddiq*, “in the right”. Pharaoh says, “The LORD is in the right (*tsaddiq*), and I and my people are in the wrong (*resha'im*)” (Exodus 9:27).

The verb *hirshia* (הִרְשִׁיעַ) means “to **declare guilty, condemn**”: it is the judge's verdict. “If there is a dispute between men and they come into court… the judges **justify the righteous and condemn the wicked**” (Deuteronomy 25:1). Turning this upside down is terrible: “He who justifies the wicked and he who **condemns the righteous** are both alike an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15).

The servant of the LORD says with confidence, “He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me?… Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; **who will declare me guilty?**” (Isaiah 50:8–9). Paul seems to echo these words: “It is God who justifies. **Who is to condemn?**” (Romans 8:33–34).

Another word belongs here: *naqah* (נָקָה), “to be clean, innocent”, and in court, “to **acquit**, leave unpunished”. God “forgives iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means **clear** the guilty” (Exodus 34:7).

sections.h: Asham and avon: guilt that must be repaired
p: *Asham* (אָשָׁם) means **guilt** and also the **guilt offering** or **reparation offering** (Leviticus 5:14–6:7). When someone had wronged another person or misused something holy, he had to **repay in full and add a fifth** (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7), and then bring an *asham* offering. Guilt in Hebrew is not first a feeling; it is a **debt** that leaves damage, and the damage must be repaired.

The verb *ashem* (אָשֵׁם) means “to be guilty” or “to bear guilt”: “if the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally… and they **realise their guilt**” (Leviticus 4:13). Even the Philistines, when they returned the ark, sent an *asham* as compensation (1 Samuel 6:3). Everyone in that world understood that guilt creates a debt that must be paid back.

*Avon* (עָוֹן), often “iniquity”, means the wrong act, the **guilt** it brings and its **consequence**, all in one word. Cain says, “My punishment (*avon*) is greater than I can bear” (Genesis 4:13). On the Day of Atonement the goat “shall bear all their iniquities on itself” (Leviticus 16:22), and of the servant Isaiah says, “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).
> Most strikingly, Isaiah 53:10 says the servant makes his life an *asham*: the offering that repairs what was broken.

sections.h: Musar in Isaiah 53:5: chastisement, discipline or punishment?
p: Isaiah 53:5 says: *musar shelomenu alav* (מוּסַר שְׁלוֹמֵנוּ עָלָיו). The **KJV** has “the **chastisement** of our peace was upon him”, the **ESV** “upon him was the **chastisement** that brought us peace”, and the **NIV** “the **punishment** that brought us peace was on him”.

Everywhere else *musar* means **discipline, correction, instruction**: “Hear, my son, your father's **instruction**” (Proverbs 1:8); “do not despise the LORD's **discipline**” (Proverbs 3:11). It is the training a father gives. The Septuagint here uses *paideia* (παιδεία), “child-training”. The NIV's “punishment” reflects the context of suffering, wounds and bearing sins, and many scholars read the verse that way.

So the verse can be heard in two ways that belong together. The servant suffers the painful discipline that should have been ours, and the result is our **shalom**, our peace and wholeness: “with his wounds we are **healed**.” The aim of this *musar* is healing and peace, not only paying a penalty. Translators must choose one English word, so it helps to know the Hebrew holds both the pain and the healing purpose.

sections.h: The Greek words: judging is not the same as condemning
p: The basic Greek verb is *krinō* (κρίνω): to **separate, decide, judge**. Its nouns are *krima* (κρίμα), a **decision or verdict**, and *krisis* (κρίσις), **judging, judgment** and also **justice** (Matthew 23:23, “justice and mercy and faithfulness”). Judging can end well or badly: God's judgment can mean putting things right for the oppressed.

*Katakrinō* (κατακρίνω) adds *kata*, “against”: to **judge against, condemn**. Its noun *katakrima* (κατάκριμα) is the **sentence of condemnation**, and in legal papyri it can mean the penalty that follows. “There is therefore now **no condemnation** for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Note what God did condemn: “he **condemned sin** in the flesh” (Romans 8:3). The verdict fell on sin, not on those who belong to Christ.

*Enochos* (ἔνοχος) means **liable, subject to** a penalty or court: “whoever murders will be **liable to judgment**” (Matthew 5:21–22). *Hypodikos* (ὑπόδικος) means **answerable to a court**: the law speaks “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be **held accountable to God**” (Romans 3:19).

*Paideuō* (παιδεύω), from *pais*, “child”, means **to train a child**, and so to discipline. “The Lord **disciplines** the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6, quoting Proverbs 3:12). But the same verb is used by Pilate: “I will therefore **punish** and release him” (Luke 23:16), meaning a Roman flogging. Its range runs from loving training to harsh beating; the context decides.

sections.h: What translators miss — and why
p: One verse shows the Greek distinctions clearly: “when we are **judged** (*krinomenoi*) by the Lord, we are **disciplined** (*paideuometha*) so that we may not be **condemned** (*katakrithōmen*) along with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:32). Judging, discipline and condemnation are three different things. But just before, the **KJV** says the unworthy eater “eateth and drinketh **damnation** to himself” (11:29), where the Greek is *krima*, “judgment”. The **ESV** and **NIV** say “judgment”.

Why “damnation”? The English word comes from Latin *damnare*, a legal word for sentencing or fining someone, and in older English “damnation” could mean any condemning sentence. Over time it narrowed to “eternal punishment in hell”, so verses like John 5:29 KJV, “the resurrection of **damnation**” (*krisis*, ESV “judgment”), now sound harsher than the Greek. Modern versions changed the word because the English changed.

In John 3:17 most versions say God did not send his Son “to **condemn** the world”, though the verb is *krinō*, “judge”. Here the context makes “condemn” a fair reading, since verse 18 contrasts it with being saved. In Romans 3:19 the **KJV** says “that all the world may become **guilty** before God”, while the **ESV** and **NIV** say “held **accountable**”: *hypodikos* means standing answerable in court, before the verdict.

In Exodus 34:7 the **KJV** prints “**the guilty**” in italics, because those words are not in the Hebrew. Literally it says “and clearing, he will not clear”. Translators add “the guilty” to make sense in English, and the italics honestly show it.

sections.h: The culture behind the words
p: In Israel, justice was done **at the city gate**, where elders sat to hear cases (Ruth 4:1–2; Amos 5:15, “establish justice in the gate”). A verdict needed **two or three witnesses** (Deuteronomy 19:15). In later times the Sanhedrin judged serious cases. Jewish law was famous for its caution: the Mishnah says a court that put someone to death once in seven years was called destructive, and one sage said once in seventy years (Mishnah Makkot 1:10).

Guilt was also communal and practical. Wrongs against a neighbour were repaired by **restitution**, as Zacchaeus promised: “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). In an **honour and shame** culture, being condemned in public at the gate was a deep shame, and being vindicated was restored honour.

The prophet Zechariah sees a courtroom in heaven. Joshua the high priest stands in filthy clothes, and “the Satan” (literally “the accuser”) stands ready to accuse him. But the LORD rebukes the accuser, and says, “Remove the filthy garments… **I have taken your iniquity away** from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:1–4). Revelation calls Satan “the accuser of our brothers” (Revelation 12:10).

In the Roman world, a magistrate sat on a raised platform, the *bēma* (Acts 18:12; 25:6), and pronounced the sentence. Greek *paideia* was the whole education of a child, and a household slave called the *paidagōgos* walked boys to school and disciplined them; Paul says the law was “our guardian until Christ came” (Galatians 3:24).

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles: no condemnation
p: Jesus said, “God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17), and “whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me… does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life” (John 5:24). In a well-loved passage (missing from the earliest manuscripts of John), Jesus asks the woman accused of adultery, “Has no one **condemned** you?… Neither do I **condemn** you; go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:10–11). No condemnation does not mean no change.

Paul's “no condemnation” (Romans 8:1) rests on a Jewish courtroom hope: God himself is the Judge who justifies, so no accuser can make a charge stick (Romans 8:33–34). The verdict “in the wrong” has been answered by the servant who became an *asham* and bore our *avon*.

Hebrews then speaks as a father: “It is for **discipline** that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons… he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:7, 10). Chastening is not condemnation. It is the **musar** of a loving Father, training his children.

sections.h: Living it out
p: If you belong to Christ, you can refuse the voice of the accuser. Guilt is real, and when you have wronged someone the biblical way is to admit it and **repair** what you can, as the *asham* laws taught. But you do not need to live under a sentence of condemnation.

When life is hard, do not assume that God is punishing you in anger. He may be training you, as a father trains a child, for your good. And let this shape how you treat others: be slow to condemn, quick to restore, and remember that God's judging aims to put things right.

quiz.why: The Greek krima means judgment; “damnation” has since narrowed to mean eternal punishment.

terms.def: To declare guilty or condemn; a judge's verdict that someone is in the wrong.
Guilt; also the guilt or reparation offering that went with restitution.
Discipline, correction and instruction, especially a father's training.
Condemnation: a sentence against someone and its penalty (Romans 8:1).
Judging, judgment, and also justice; not always a negative verdict.
Answerable to a court, held accountable (Romans 3:19).
To train a child; to discipline or chasten, sometimes to flog.
